children: There are three things about the shares of Tata Sons which everyone in the world of business knows – these are shares of a privately held company, the shares cannot be transferred and they cannot be liquidated or relinquished.

None of these conditions, as laid out in the articles of association of Tata Sons, is ultra vires the law; meaning the manner in which the shares of Tata Sons have been structured is in compliance with the law. Normally, no lender will be willing to accept such shares as a security, knowing very well their illiquid nature.

Yet, large, marquee, global private credit funds and foreign banks have lent to the Shapoorji Pallonji Group, accepting shares of Tata Sons as security. Foreign lenders, ranging from Deutsche Bank to Davidson Kempner to Cerberus Capital form a majority of total external liabilities of the group.

That the loans have been rolled over multiple times (at rates upwards of 14%) doesn’t offer comfort. No wonder then, Rs 60,000 crore plus of debt exposure has snowballed to a massive existential crisis for the conglomerate.
Listing shouldn’t be a way of giving an exit
Shares of Tata Sons are being held as hostage to solve the problem.
This is unfair.

For one, this is not the first time that India has faced a massive credit risk. But this is the first time that the system is trying to bend backwards to solve the issue. The Reserve Bank of India, whose primary function is to safeguarding public money, has taken on itself the task of imposing the listing of Tata Sons shares.

Legal definitions are being written and rewritten to ensure that they are justified in pushing Tata Sons towards listing. For an institution that cares a lot about setting precedent, this is giving a wrong message.

India Inc still has many unlisted ultimate holding companies which circulate money within the group in fancy structures. Why single out Tata Sons when it has promised to abide by the rules of the land to distance itself from any form of financing activity whether for itself or its group companies?
The only logical reason to push for listing then has to be to solve for the debt woes of a minority shareholder- it holds a little over 18 percent stake in Tata Sons.
Bad credit call
Offering solutions to minority shareholders was never the lookout of RBI and it shouldn’t make it one now either.
Every lender knew the risk of underwriting shares of Tata Sons and yet they did it.

Whether Davidson Kempner or Cerberus, they should own up for their bad underwriting calls rather than moving the mountains to get a backdoor exit. If anything, the RBI should hold up a mirror to these private credit funds and call out their due diligence instead of bowing down to their demands.

It is not that that regulator hasn’t done it in the past, but this time around for strange reasons, a likely default by the SP Group (should that happen) is already getting tagged as a possible sovereign default.
Not an acceptable argument
That’s a bad stand to take.
Though very limited in numbers, India has had instances of government backed companies defaulting loans to domestic banks. These haven’t mothballed into a sovereign issue in the past.
Why should SP Group’s case be any different and that too when it is not even a government backed entity or a group that enjoys sovereign rating.

Rating on most SP Group companies is BBB minus. As per ICRA’s latest report on Shapoorji Pallonji & Company Private Limited which has a near Rs 20,000 crore exposure to lenders, the credit rating agency while ascribing BBB minus (BBB-) with a negative outlook said “the negative outlook reflects ICRA’s expectation that the company’s credit profile is likely to remain under pressure in the medium term, on the backdrop of subdued performance in the core EPC business, stretched liquidity and weak debt coverage metrics”.
This implies that the troubled financial position is on account weak business performance.

It further strengthens the case for why shares of Tata Sons should not be used as a pawn to make good for SP Group’s huge loans, whether by way of listing or even a partial exit. When the creditors knew the risk involved in the security offered, arm-twisting the system and polarizing opinions within one of India’s leading corporate groups will not result in a lasting solution.

Tata Trusts and Noel Tata shouldn’t take the bait. But should they succumb to pressure, hope they remember that SP Group doesn’t enjoy the brightest credit rating to seek valuation on their stake in Tata Sons at market price or above.

title: Vault Matters | Tata Sons shouldn’t be held hostage for bad credit underwriting
